Extensor Mechanism Injuries
 CORE
November 29, 2022
Eli T. Sayegh, MD
Simon Görtz, MD
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define quadriceps and patellar tendon injuries and their epidemiology, including predisposing
factors.
Review the conceptual foundation of extensor mechanism injuries, including their anatomy,
biomechanics, and pathomechanics.
Summarize the clinical manifestations of extensor mechanism injuries, including patient
presentation, physical examination, and factors unique to incomplete or chronic ruptures.
Review the characteristics of these injuries on radiographs and MRIs.
Explain the management of these injuries, beginning with acute management and ending with
surgical repair and postoperative rehabilitation.
Discuss the fundamentals of surgical technique and potential complications.

Definition
Acute rupture of the patellar or quadriceps tendon, typically at or near the osteotendinous
junction, often is caused by eccentric contraction while loading the knee during flexion
Most patients report acute pain, a subjective popping sensation, hemarthrosis presenting as
effusion and soft-tissue swelling, and inability to actively extend the knee. Physical
examination findings include a palpable defect and inability to perform resisted knee
extension or a straight leg raise.
Epidemiology
Quadriceps tendon ruptures are more common than patellar tendon ruptures, with an
incidence of 1.37 and 0.68 per 100,000 person-years, respectively.1 Males are more commonly
affected than females.
Quadriceps tendon ruptures are more common in patients older than 40 years and patellar
tendon ruptures are more common in patients younger than 40 years.2,3
Preexisting degenerative tendinopathy frequently is present in patients who sustain repetitive
microtrauma.

Epidemiology
Other than preexisting tendinopathy or prior injury, risk factors include systemic
administration or local injection of corticosteroid, diabetes mellitus, renal failure,
rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, connective-tissue disorders, and
fluoroquinolone use. Less commonly, patellar tendon rupture may be a complication
after total knee arthroplasty or anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with patellar or
quadriceps tendon autograft harvest.
Anatomy
The quadriceps tendon is the confluence of the rectus femoris (superficial), vastus medialis
and vastus lateralis (middle), and vastus intermedius (deep; Figure 1). The musculotendinous

junction is approximately 3 cm proximal to the superior patellar pole.
Figure 1 Illustration shows the anatomy of the extensor mechanism. (Reproduced from
Matava MJ: Patellar tendon ruptures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1996;4[6]:287-296.)
Of these four muscles, only the rectus femoris, which originates at the anterior inferior iliac
spine and the hip capsule, crosses the hip joint.
The vastus medialis and vastus lateralis are contiguous with tendinous expansions known as
the medial retinaculum and the lateral retinaculum, respectively, which insert onto the medial
and lateral aspects of the superior patellar pole and the proximal tibia. The patellar tendon is
confluent with these retinacula medially and laterally.
A layer of synovium is deep to the quadriceps tendon and accounts for the large hemarthrosis
if torn.
The patella functions as a fulcrum because of its anterior position, increasing the lever arm of
the quadriceps relative to the joint center of rotation.
The mean anterior-posterior thickness of the quadriceps tendon is 7 to 8 mm.4
The mean anterior-posterior thickness of the patellar tendon is 4 mm, and its proximal width
mirrors that of the patella. It thickens to 5 to 6 mm and narrows at its insertion on the tibial
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Extensor Mechanism Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001180
3/16

tubercle.3
The major vascular supplies of the patellar tendon are the infrapatellar fat pad and the
retinacular structures.5 The proximal and distal attachments of the patellar tendon are
relatively avascular and most prone to rupture.3
Biomechanics
The ratio of force transmitted through the patellar tendon relative to the quadriceps tendon is
more than 1.0 in less than 45° flexion and less than 1.0 in more than 45° flexion. At higher
flexion angles (>60°), forces on the patellar tendon are greatest.6
At lower flexion angles, the patellofemoral contact point (or fulcrum) is at the inferior patellar
pole, giving the quadriceps tendon a longer lever arm and mechanical advantage.6 Deeper in
flexion, the patellofemoral contact area shifts proximally, giving the patellar tendon a
mechanical advantage during knee extension.
In addition to the degree of knee flexion, the ability of the patella to tilt in the sagittal plane
affects the relative force in each tendon.
Pathomechanics of Injury
Most injuries occur as the extensor mechanism contracts eccentrically (as the muscle
lengthens), which generates higher forces than during concentric contraction. This often
occurs in combination with loading the knee in flexion with full body weight, but it also may
occur after a direct blow to the knee.
The quadriceps or patellar tendon typically avulses off the patella because of considerably
increased strain at the tendon-bone interface.
The forces required to rupture a normal patellar tendon are 17 times body weight7 or 3 times
body weight if ascending stairs.8
Injuries to the quadriceps or patellar tendon typically propagate through the medial and/or
lateral retinacula, causing global disruption of the extensor hood.
Deformation because of tensile load is substantially higher at the proximal and distal
attachments of the patellar tendon than within the midsubstance.9 Therefore, most ruptures
occur at the bone-tendon junction.
Any layer of the trilaminar quadriceps tendon structure may be torn. Accurate characterization
of the three-dimensional tear pattern, including delamination of individual layers is important.

Tendon rupture is indicative of preexisting tendinopathy because tensile overload of the
extensor mechanism in the experimental setting of a healthy tendon leads to bony failure at
the patella.10 This is corroborated by the findings of a histopathologic study showing the
universal presence of pathologic changes in spontaneously ruptured patellar tendons
compared with only one-third of intact control tendons.11 Similarly, in the quadriceps tendon,
approximately 75% of the fibers must be cut for rupture to occur under physiologic forces,
reinforcing the paradigm that a weakened tendon precedes rupture.
Although surgically repaired tendons form tendon callus and remodel over 3 to 6 months to
form an organized structure akin to a normal tendon,12 neglected ruptures bridge the zone of
injury with scar tissue and result in a lengthened, biomechanically inefficient tendon.
Clinical Presentation
The patient may report sudden pain with a subjective pop or tearing sensation, with inability to
bear weight on the injured limb and development of a hemarthrosis.
Physical examination reveals tenderness and/or a palpable gap at the site of rupture,
increased vertical mobility of the patella, weakness of resisted knee extension, and inability to
perform a straight leg raise.
Patients may exhibit knee extension with an extensor lag if continuity of the medial or
retinaculum or compensation from the iliotibial band, which crosses the knee anteriorly to its
center of rotation, is present.
In patients with subacute or chronic injuries, the tendon defect may be obscured by mature
hematoma and scar tissue.
Imaging Studies
Lateral radiographs demonstrate patella baja or patella alta for quadriceps or patellar tendon
ruptures (Figure 2), respectively, which can be measured using the Insall-Salvati ratio, the
Caton-Deschamps index, or the Blackburne-Peel ratio. If the extensor mechanism is intact, the
inferior pole of the patella should normally be at the level of the Blumensaat line with the knee
in 30° flexion. A sunrise view may further demonstrate asymmetry of the patellofemoral joint
relative to the contralateral knee.

Figure 2 Lateral knee radiograph shows patella alta consistent with patellar tendon rupture,
with the patella positioned cephalad to the Blumensaat line. (Reproduced from Matava MJ:
Patellar tendon ruptures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1996;4[6]:287-296.)
Radiographs also may demonstrate obliteration of the quadriceps/patellar tendon shadow and
a suprapatellar/infrapatellar mass or calcific density.
Avulsion fractures should be identified if present.
MRI is not necessary for diagnosis in patents with unequivocal physical examination findings;
however, it can differentiate incomplete ruptures from complete ruptures. It also may be a
useful adjunct for surgical planning.
MRI findings, seen observed on sagittal views, include discontinuity and/or tortuous course of
tendon fibers and an increased signal intensity on T2-weighted and other fluid-sensitive views
(Figure 3).

6/16

Figure 3 T1-weighted sagittal MRI of a knee shows discontinuity of the ruptured quadriceps
tendon (arrow), the appearance of increased laxity of the patellar tendon because of patella
baja, and decreased resting patellar tendon tension. (Reproduced from Ilan DI, Tejwani N,
Keschner M, Leibman M: Quadriceps tendon rupture. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2003;11[3]:192-
200.)
Ultrasonography is a highly sensitive and specific imaging modality that can characterize the
location of injury and differentiate between partial and complete ruptures; however, its utility
is operator-dependent. Complete ruptures will exhibit a gap between the free tendon ends
with an intercalary hematoma, which appears hypoechoic or anechoic.
Treatment Options
Management of these injuries in the emergency department includes the following:

AAOS | Extensor Mechanism Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001180
7/16

Ruling out other intraarticular knee injuries with similar mechanisms of injury (eg, anterior
cruciate ligament injury, meniscal tear, osteochondral fracture, and/or patellar dislocation)
Application of a knee immobilizer or a hinged knee brace locked in extension.
Occasionally, if the physical examination is obscured by pain, the hemarthrosis may be
aspirated and the knee injected with ropivacaine or another less chondrotoxic local anesthetic.
Because a joint effusion adversely affects quadriceps strength, the use of ice; compression;
NSAIDs; and, occasionally, needle evacuation of the hemarthrosis (before it consolidates) may
be advised to reduce the knee effusion.
Nonsurgical treatment typically is appropriate for patients who have an incomplete rupture
with continuity of the extensor mechanism (with intact straight leg raise) and patients who are
medically unfit for surgical treatment.
Incomplete ruptures are managed via immobilization of the knee in full extension for 6 weeks,
followed by protected range-of-motion and strengthening exercises.
Patients with a complete rupture should undergo surgical treatment in a timely fashion to
optimize the prognosis, ideally within 2 weeks postinjury13 or pending improvement of soft-
tissue swelling. Delayed repair increases the risk of subnormal quadriceps strength and loss of
full knee motion.
Timely recognition of quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures is important to facilitate
prompt surgical management because primary repair may become more difficult and may be
subject to increased tensile forces if delayed more than 6 weeks.13-15 This is because of
tendon retraction, migration of the patella (with loss of passive patellar mobility), formation of
fibrous adhesions between the patella and the femur or tibia (depending on the tendon
ruptured), and contracture and scar-tissue encasement of the torn tendon end. In addition,
the incongruent resting position of the patella may precipitate injury to the patellofemoral
articular surfaces.
Surgical Technique
An offset midline surgical approach is used, with development of full-thickness flaps medially
and laterally and exposure of the quadriceps or patellar tendon, patella, and retinaculum.
The quadriceps or patellar tendon stump is retrieved, and retinacular tears are identified.
The hematoma is evacuated, and the knee joint is copiously irrigated.
The tendon edge is sharply débrided, and the patellar footprint is roughened to facilitate a
bleeding cancellous bed for healing.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Extensor Mechanism Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001180
8/16

Repair of the ruptured quadriceps or patellar tendon is performed with the use of heavy
nonabsorbable suture or suture tape in a running, locking Krackow or Bunnell configuration.
Passage and fixation of the suture repair is commonly performed with the use of transosseous
tunnels (Figure 4) or suture anchors, which are associated with similar biomechanical
properties with less surgical dissection.16
Figure 4 Illustration of a knee shows the surgical technique for four-stranded locking Krackow
quadriceps tendon repair, which is passed (via a Keith needle or a Beath pin) through three 2-
mm parallel longitudinal transosseous tunnels and tied over the inferior patellar pole.
(Adapted with permission from Azar FM, Pickering RM: Traumatic disorders, in Canale ST, ed:
Campbell’s Operative Orthopaedics, ed 9. St Louis, MO, Mosby, 1998, vol 2, p 1430.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Extensor Mechanism Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001180
9/16

Medial and retinacular tears are repaired.
The knee is taken through an arc of 0° to 90° of flexion to assess patellofemoral tracking and
ensure no excess tension or gapping is present at the repair site.
Tenuous quadriceps tendon repairs may be augmented via the Scuderi technique (quadriceps
flap turndown).17 A partial-thickness triangular flap of the anterior proximal tendon is
reflected distally over the repair site and tied with the use of sutures at the base and along
each side.
Rehabilitation
Immediately postoperatively, the patient usually is permitted to bear weight as tolerated in a
hinged knee brace locked in extension. For repairs of chronic ruptures, a more conservative
rehabilitation plan may be advisable.
During the first 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively, the knee may be maintained in full extension
(particularly during ambulation) or allowed protected early range of motion (active flexion and
passive extension in the prone position) before the patient begins a progressive active range-
of-motion protocol.
Use of crutches may be discontinued after the patient displays sufficient quadriceps control.
A supervised physical therapy regimen should incorporate active flexion and passive extension
exercises. After restoration of supple joint motion, isokinetic closed chain strengthening
exercises are initiated, followed by a sport-specific functional rehabilitation program.
Restoration of a satisfactory arc of motion should be expected by 12 to 16 weeks
postoperatively.
The patient may be cleared for strenuous exercise 4 to 6 months postoperatively after
demonstrating a full arc of motion and 85% to 90% the isokinetic strength of the contralateral
lower extremity.
Complications
The most common complications include quadriceps weakness, persistent extensor lag, and
loss of knee flexion.
Manipulation under anesthesia may be considered if the patient lacks 120° of flexion 8 weeks
postoperatively.
Wound complications, although infrequent, most often involve the distal aspect of the incision
the location at which the soft-tissue envelope is thinnest. Placing the incision just lateral to the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Extensor Mechanism Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001180
10/16

tibial tubercle, the location at which the skin is thicker and better vascularized, may mitigate
this problem.
Persistence of a knee effusion will adversely affect quadriceps strength.
Re-rupture may occur in running or jumping athletes who return to sport before tendon
healing is complete.
Inaccurate repair tension or nonanatomic tendon reattachment may cause patella baja or
patella alta, depending on the tendon repaired, resulting in motion loss and incongruence of
the patellofemoral joint.
Chronic Tendon Ruptures
Special attention should be given to detecting chronic or neglected extensor mechanism
injuries. These patients may present with extensor lag and/or fixed retraction of the
quadriceps or the patellar tendon. Left unmanaged, the tendon remains retracted and heals
with scar tissue, resulting in a lengthened, inefficient musculotendinous unit.
The outcomes of the surgical management of chronic ruptures generally are less favorable
than those of ruptures managed in a timely fashion.14,17-19
Primary repair may be performed if the tendon ends remain apposed. If tendon retraction has
resulted in a substantial gap, the first goal is mobilize the tendon and release adhesions from
the underlying bone, soft tissues, and skin to restore length. Scar tissue should be excised to a
viable tendon edge. The surgeon should be familiar with the armamentarium of reconstruction
options.
V-Y lengthening and/or augmentation with allograft may be necessary for tendon stumps that
have retracted more than 5 cm. If V-Y lengthening is performed, the length of the limbs of the
V should be double the length of the defect.
Codivilla lengthening is a reconstructive technique for the management of chronic quadriceps
tendon ruptures, in which a full-thickness triangular turndown flap of the quadriceps is
brought down 1.3 to 2.0 cm proximal to the level of the tear2 (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Illustrations of knees show the Codivilla lengthening technique for the management
of chronic quadriceps tendon rupture. A, The chronic quadriceps tendon tear is exposed.
Proximal retraction prevents direct apposition no the tear. Dashed lines represent the inverted
V-shaped cut to be made. B, The full-thickness triangular turndown flap is fashioned. The
inverted V-shaped cut allows the tera to be approximated and repaired. C, The proximal limbs
are repaired side to side, and the distal flap is brought distally to bridge the tendon gap.
(Adapted with permission from Scuderi C: Ruptures of the quadriceps tendon: Study of twenty
tendon ruptures. Am J Surg 1958;95[4]:626-634.)
Options for allograft reconstruction include fascia lata, semitendinosus, gracilis, or Achilles
tendon, with or without a bone block (Figure 6).

Figure 6 Lateral (A) and AP (B) view illustrations of a knee show reconstruction of a chronic
patellar tendon rupture with the use of Achilles tendon allograft with bone block, which is
secured to a rectangular bed within the tibial tubercle with the use of two 3.5-mm cortical
screws. (Adapted with permission from Wiesel SW, ed: Operative Techniques in Orthopaedic
Surgery. Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2012.
Drop-lock knee bracing is a consideration for injuries that cannot be managed surgically or
patients who are medically unfit for surgical treatment. This type of hinged knee brace locks
the knee in full extension and then uses a spring-loaded drop-lock lever to allow for full
flexion.
Other Abnormalities of the Extensor Mechanism
Patellar tendinopathy (jumper knee) is common in jumping athletes, such as basketball and
volleyball players, causing pain in the inferior patellar pole or proximal patellar tendon. The
primary etiology is degenerative rather than inflammatory because of repetitive stresses
transmitted through the extensor mechanism. The Blazina classification20 stratifies patients
into three categories according to symptom occurrence after and/or during exercise, symptom
occurrence without exercise, and deterioration of performance. Radiographs may reveal
calcification within the tendon, elongation or fragmentation of the inferior patellar pole,
and/or a so-called tooth sign of the anterior patella because of periosteal reaction. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Extensor Mechanism Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001180
13/16

mainstay of management is activity modification, NSAIDs, physical therapy emphasizing an
eccentric exercise program, and a Cho-Pat strap (Medi-Dyne) to reduce patellar tendon
tension. Cortisone injections should be strictly avoided because of rupture risk.
Osgood-Schlatter syndrome is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, which is a secondary
ossification center. This condition is a source of anterior knee pain during adolescence and is
more common in boys. The etiology is repetitive stresses encountered by the extensor
mechanism during activities such as jumping, sprinting, or kneeling. Radiographs demonstrate
irregularity and fragmentation of the tibial tubercle, and MRI is not necessary for diagnosis.
This condition typically is self-limiting by skeletal maturity and is managed via activity
modifications, NSAIDs, and physical therapy. In rare patients, surgical excision of the
symptomatic ossicle is necessary.
Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome is a traction apophysitis of the inferior patellar pole,
which occurs during adolescence and has a similar pathogenesis to Osgood-Schlatter
syndrome. It typically is self-limiting and resolves with nonsurgical management.
Mark as Complete
